title: Cardiac cycle: pressures, volume, and valve events
concept: Relate the four phases of the left-ventricular cycle to mitral/aortic valve opening and closing, heart sounds, and the Wiggers pressure and volume tracings.

storyboard.caption: Isovolumetric contraction: mitral valve closes (S1). Pressure rises steeply while volume stays constant.
Ejection: LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens, and volume falls to end-systolic volume.
Isovolumetric relaxation: aortic valve closes (S2). Pressure falls while volume is constant again.
Filling: when LV pressure drops below atrial pressure the mitral valve opens; rapid filling, then the atrial kick.

title: Ventricular myocyte action potential
concept: Phases 0-4 with the ion currents responsible and the antiarrhythmic classes that act on each.

storyboard.caption: Phase 0: fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open; Na+ rushes in and the membrane depolarizes to about +20 mV. Class I drugs slow this upstroke.
Phase 1: Na+ channels inactivate; a transient outward K+ current (Ito) produces the small notch.
Phase 2 plateau: L-type Ca2+ influx balances K+ efflux, holding the membrane near 0 mV. Class IV (Ca2+ blockers) shortens it; Ca2+ entry triggers contraction.
Phase 3: Ca2+ channels close while delayed-rectifier K+ currents (IKr, IKs) repolarize the cell. Class III drugs block these and prolong the QT.
Phase 4: resting potential near -90 mV, set by inward-rectifier K+ (IK1) and the Na+/K+ ATPase. The cell is refractory until Na+ channels recover.

title: Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts
concept: Why the curve is sigmoid and how CO2, H+, temperature, 2,3-BPG and CO shift it; P50 as the marker.

storyboard.caption: Cooperative binding gives a sigmoid curve. P50, the PO2 at 50% saturation, is about 26 mm Hg. Arterial blood (~100 mm Hg) is ~98% saturated; mixed venous (~40 mm Hg) ~75%.
Right shift: higher P50, lower affinity, more O2 unloaded to tissue. Causes: increased CO2, H+ (acidosis), temperature, 2,3-BPG, exercise, altitude.
Left shift: lower P50, higher affinity, less unloading. Causes: decreased CO2, alkalosis, hypothermia, low 2,3-BPG, fetal hemoglobin, methemoglobin.
Carbon monoxide: binds heme ~250x more avidly than O2, lowering O2 content, and shifts the remaining curve left so even bound O2 is released poorly.

title: Coagulation cascade: intrinsic, extrinsic, common pathways
concept: See the sequence of factor activation, where PT and PTT measure, and where warfarin, heparin and DOACs act.

storyboard.caption: Extrinsic pathway: vessel injury exposes tissue factor, which binds factor VIIa. TF-VIIa activates X (and some IX). Measured by the PT / INR.
Intrinsic pathway: contact activation of XII leads to XIa, then IXa, which with its cofactor VIIIa activates X. Measured by the aPTT.
Common pathway: Xa with Va converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa); thrombin cleaves fibrinogen (I) to fibrin, and XIIIa cross-links the clot.

Drug targets: warfarin blocks synthesis of II, VII, IX, X (PT rises first because VII is shortest-lived); heparin potentiates antithrombin against IIa and Xa; DOACs inhibit Xa (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or IIa (dabigatran).

title: Moving the test cutoff: sensitivity vs specificity
concept: Two overlapping distributions and a sliding threshold showing how TP, FP, TN and FN change, and the resulting ROC curve.

storyboard.caption: Test values overlap between healthy (blue) and diseased (red) people. A cutoff splits each group into true/false positives and negatives.
Lowering the cutoff catches more disease (sensitivity rises, fewer false negatives) at the cost of more false positives (specificity falls). Use for screening and rule-out.
Raising the cutoff does the opposite: specificity rises, sensitivity falls. Use for confirmation and rule-in. Sensitivity and specificity do not depend on prevalence.
Sweeping the cutoff traces the ROC curve (sensitivity vs 1 - specificity). Area under the curve summarizes discrimination; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.

title: Nephron: where sodium, water, and solutes are handled
concept: Follow filtrate along the nephron and see which transporters act in each segment and which diuretics block them.

storyboard.caption: Proximal tubule reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na+ and water isosmotically (SGLT2, NHE3, carbonic anhydrase). Acetazolamide acts here. Glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate are largely reclaimed.
Loop of Henle: thin descending limb is water-permeable; thick ascending limb is water-impermeable and reabsorbs Na/K/2Cl via NKCC2. Loop diuretics (furosemide) block NKCC2 — the 'diluting segment'.
Distal convoluted tubule: NCC (Na-Cl cotransporter) reabsorbs ~5–10% of Na+. Thiazides block NCC. This is also where PTH-regulated calcium reabsorption occurs.
Collecting duct: principal cells use ENaC (blocked by amiloride; aldosterone increases ENaC) and AQP2 water channels (ADH). Intercalated cells secrete H+. Spironolactone antagonises aldosterone.

title: Left ventricular pressure-volume loop
concept: Trace the PV loop counter-clockwise, identify EDV, ESV, stroke volume and how preload, afterload and contractility change the loop.

storyboard.caption: Trace the loop counter-clockwise: filling (bottom), isovolumetric contraction (right), ejection (top), isovolumetric relaxation (left). Width is stroke volume (EDV − ESV).
Increased preload: the loop widens to the right. EDV rises, stroke volume rises (Frank–Starling) if afterload and contractility are unchanged.
Increased afterload: the loop grows taller and narrower. ESV rises, stroke volume falls. Hypertension is the clinical example.
Increased contractility: the end-systolic pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR) steepens, ESV falls, stroke volume rises. Inotropes and exercise.
